The embryonic development of the sea lamprey Petromyzon marinus begins within a simple nest constructed by spawning adults in gravel-bottomed streams. Following fertilisation, the fertilised ovum proceeds through cleavage and gastrulation as an externally developing yolk-dependent embryo. At a water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, marked by the first feeding of the filter-feeding larva (ammocoete), occurs approximately 35 days [ab = approximately 35 days] after fertilisation. The emerging larva weighs only 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] on a dry-weight basis, a mass that derives from an egg diameter of about one millimetre. This slight initial dry mass belies the extraordinary growth potential of the species, as the ammocoete will spend several years burrowing in soft sediments before undergoing the radical metamorphosis that transforms it into a parasitic juvenile. The incubation duration is relatively brief compared to the protracted larval phase, a life-history strategy that emphasises rapid hatching and the exploitation of sheltered nursery habitats.

After spending a prolonged period as a filter-feeding larva, the sea lamprey undergoes a dramatic metamorphosis into a parasitic juvenile that migrates to the ocean or large lakes. The age at which individuals attain the size necessary to initiate this transformation is linked to the onset of reproductive maturation, which is defined by the achievement of a total length of 13.6 centimetres [Lp = 13.6 centimetres]. This measurement represents the length at puberty, after which the animal ceases somatic growth in preparation for its adult feeding phase. The total length at puberty is a critical life-history threshold because it signals the end of the sub-adult period and the beginning of the aggressive parasitic phase that will fuel future reproductive investment. In many freshwater systems, lampreys achieving this size are already transitioning to an actively feeding mode, attaching to host fishes with their oral sucker. The growth trajectory leading to this point is heavily influenced by local temperature and prey availability, with individuals in richer environments reaching this milestone more rapidly than those in oligotrophic habitats.

The parasitic feeding phase of adult Petromyzon marinus is characterised by remarkable somatic expansion, during which individuals attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 2300 grams [Wwi = approximately 2300 grams]. This maximum adult body mass is achieved after a period of intense hematophagous feeding on large-bodied teleosts and marine mammals, a strategy that supports rapid lipid and protein accumulation. The ultimate total length corresponding to this mass extent is approximately 120 centimetres [Li = approximately 120 centimetres], a size that marks the end of the active growth phase. Field records indicate that individuals reaching this asymptotic size have invested heavily in somatic tissue, building the reserves necessary for the upcoming spawning migration. This migratory journey is energetically demanding, as lampreys cease feeding entirely once they enter freshwater to spawn. The massive investment in adult body size reflects a life-history strategy where a single, terminal reproductive event is fuelled entirely by energy stored during the parasitic phase. Somatic death follows shortly after spawning, completing the semelparous life cycle.

Reproductive output in sea lamprey is remarkably high, reflecting its semelparous life-history strategy where all resources are allocated to a single breeding event. At a water temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C], a single gravid female can produce approximately 100,000 eggs  at the end of life, a fecundity that is among the highest recorded for any species of comparable body size. The first reproduction event of the lamprey occurs after a prolonged period of development and feeding. The age at first spawning is estimated to be 5 years following fertilisation [tR = 5 years following fertilisation], again at an ambient temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C] for the riverine spawning grounds. This five-year delay between birth and spawning allows the animal to pass through all larval and juvenile stages, complete the parasitic feeding phase, and migrate back to natal streams. The synchronisation of spawning with spring thermal regimes maximises the survival prospects of the fertilised ova and subsequent embryos, ensuring that the next generation emerges into an environment with abundant food resources.

The maximum lifespan of Petromyzon marinus is constrained by its semelparous reproductive strategy, with individuals living for a maximum of 11 years [am = 11 years] when reared at a water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This unusually long lifespan for an anadromous fish is a consequence of the extended larval and metamorphic phases. Following the complete attainment of puberty, the individual enters a non-trophic spawning phase, and physiological death occurs rapidly after the completion of gamete release. The overall cohort mortality is extremely high during the early life stages, with only a tiny fraction of the 100,000 eggs reaching sexual maturity. The species' life-history strategy is thus heavily skewed toward high fecundity as compensation for elevated pre-reproductive mortality. This energetic trade-off between ultimate adult size and reproductive investment is consistent with that observed in other parasitic and semelparous species. The early development at a cold temperature produces a larva that will spend years accumulating resources before the final, cataclysmic spawning event that ends the life cycle.
